Just now

--

Photo by Igor Omilaev on UnsplashAsk any current AI model to write learning objectives for a customer service course and, in about three seconds, you will get something like this:
Given a live customer inquiry and access to the CRM knowledge base, the associate will resolve the inquiry without escalation, achieving a first-contact resolution rate of 85% or higher.
It is a good sentence.
It has a condition. It has an observable behavior. It has a criterion. Mager would recognize the structure. Put it in a design document and most approval chains will let it sail right through.
And it may be completely, expensively wrong. Not wrong in its grammar. Wrong in its premise.
Wrong because it assumes associates escalate cases because they do not know how to resolve them. Wrong because 85% may have come from nowhere. Wrong because the CRM may return unreliable information. Wrong because the associate may not have the authority to make the decision. Wrong because the incentive system may reward short handle time instead of first-contact resolution.
The objective can be beautifully written and completely unfounded. Those are two separate things. That distinction matters now because drafting is cheap. The sentence is no longer the difficult part. A learning objective is not just a sentence.
It is a claim.
And the sentence is the cheapest part of the claim to produce.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Photo by Nick Fewings on UnsplashWhat an objective is really claiming
A performance-based objective looks compact, but it carries several assumptions inside it.
A real performance gap exists
Someone is not producing an outcome the organization needs.
That should be a factual claim. There should be a metric, a baseline, an observed failure, a quality issue, a safety concern, a customer outcome, or some other evidence that the gap actually exists.
“We need training” is not evidence.
“Leadership is concerned” is not a performance metric.
“People do not seem confident” is not a diagnosis.
The gap is caused by a deficiency in human capability
The objective assumes the performer lacks knowledge, skill, judgment, or practice.
It also assumes the problem is not primarily caused by:

• poor tools

• missing information

• inadequate staffing

• conflicting incentives

• broken processes

• unclear expectations

• insufficient authority

• unavailable resources

• bad system design

• missing feedback
That is a major assumption.
This particular behavior is the lever
Of everything the performer does, the behavior named in the objective is assumed to be the one that will improve the outcome.
Why that behavior?
What evidence connects it to the gap?
Was it observed? Did experienced performers identify it? Does the data show that failure at this step predicts the larger problem?
Or did the behavior simply sound appropriate for the course?
The criterion means something
The objective says 85%.
Why?
Why not 75%? Why not 92%? Why not zero critical errors? Why not completion within 12 minutes?
Somebody should be able to answer that question.
The criterion may come from a safety standard, regulatory requirement, engineering tolerance, operational benchmark, financial threshold, or performance level demonstrated by competent employees.
If it came from the AI because the sentence needed a number, it is not a criterion. It is decoration. The first claim requires data. The second requires diagnosis. The third requires task and performance analysis. The fourth requires operational, economic, safety, or regulatory context.
An AI system drafting from a prompt does not automatically have any of that. It has the request. It has whatever documents you supplied. It has patterns from similar language. So it produces the artifact and quietly implies that all four claims are true.
That is the trap.
The objective does not arrive with a warning label saying:
This is structurally sound but unsupported by evidence.
It arrives polished.
And fluency reads as authority.
Watch the numbers
The easiest place to see the problem is the criterion.
Ask AI to generate objectives and watch the numbers appear:

• 95% accuracy;

• within 15 minutes;

• zero critical errors;

• three out of four scenarios;

• an 85% first-contact resolution rate.
They arrive with complete confidence. Nobody argues with 95%. It sounds rigorous. But where did it come from?
A real criterion should trace to something outside the sentence.
In a clinical setting, it may come from a safety threshold. In manufacturing, from a specification tolerance. In customer service, from the point at which repeat contacts become more expensive than additional handling time. In sales, from the conversion rate required to sustain the territory.
A legitimate criterion has an owner and a source. A generated criterion often has neither. The slot wanted a number, so a number appeared. One operational habit would eliminate a great deal of nonsense:
Every number in an objective needs a source.
If nobody can name the source, mark it provisional. Do not allow an invented number to walk into a design document wearing a lab coat.
Verification is not validation
Software and systems engineering make a useful distinction.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Photo by Marek Studzinski on UnsplashVerification asks:
Did we build the thing correctly?
Is the artifact internally consistent? Does it conform to the specification? Does every component line up with the others?
Validation asks:
Did we build the correct thing?
Does the solution correspond to the actual need in the world?
Verification can often happen inside the artifact.
Validation requires contact with something outside it: the performer, the workflow, the data, the system, the customer, or the environment in which the work occurs.
AI is already good at verification.
It can check whether:

• the objective uses an observable verb

• the assessment measures the stated behavior

• the practice activity reflects the stated condition

• enabling objectives support the terminal objective

• lessons contradict one another

• an assessment measures recall when the objective requires performance

• content exists that supports no objective

• objectives exist that are never assessed
Across a large curriculum, it can perform that review faster than a human who is exhausted by module eleven.
That is real value.
But verification cannot create warrant. A perfectly aligned course teaching the wrong skill is still the wrong course. You can build a beautiful, tightly aligned, gorgeously assessed course that solves nothing.
Internal coherence is not external truth. So, can AI prove that the objective addresses the performance problem?
No. Not on its own, and not simply because the models need to improve. Proof of correspondence requires contact with the thing being corresponded to. Give the system performance data, observation notes, interview transcripts, system logs, ticket categories, and workflow evidence, and it can become a powerful reasoning partner. Without that evidence, it is producing plausible professional language.That is not the same thing as establishing that the language is true.
The diagnosis it will skip unless you require it
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Photo by Agence Olloweb on UnsplashThe performance-improvement field has known for decades that many performance problems are not training problems. Gilbert’s Behavior Engineering Model directs attention to environmental supports such as information, resources, and incentives, along with individual factors such as knowledge, capacity, and motivation.
Rummler and Brache made the same basic point at the process level: put a good performer in a bad system and the system usually wins.
Clark and Estes framed performance gaps in terms of knowledge, motivation, and organizational barriers.
Mager and Pipe gave us the bluntest diagnostic question:
Could they do it if their life depended on it?
If the answer is yes, you may not have a training problem.
Now type this into an AI system:
Write learning objectives for reducing medication administration errors.
You will get objectives.
Immediately.
You probably will not get questions about whether the errors are concentrated on a particular shift. The model may not ask whether scanner failures increased, whether labels changed, whether staffing deteriorated, or whether the reporting process punishes people for documenting near misses.
You asked for objectives. It gave you objectives. This is the professionally dangerous form of sycophancy.
Not flattery.
Frame acceptance.
You brought a training frame. The system worked inside the training frame. It did not necessarily stop to ask whether the frame was wrong.
That is why the better question is not merely:
What objective should we write?
It is:
What would have to be true for this objective to affect the performance problem?
Now you are doing analysis.
What AI can actually contribute
The useful move is to stop asking AI only to produce the objective and start asking it to attack the objective.
Used adversarial, and given real inputs, it can contribute to the evidentiary chain in several important ways.
Generate rival hypotheses
Ask it for explanations that training cannot fix:
Here is the performance gap. Generate 15 plausible non-training causes using Gilbert’s model. For each one, identify the evidence that would confirm or weaken it.
This is exactly the kind of structured divergence AI handles well. It also counters frame acceptance. You are using the system against its own default.
Surface assumptions
Give it the objective and ask:
What must be true about the performers, tools, workflow, incentives, authority, and environment for this objective to improve the stated outcome?
Then ask it to rank the assumptions by:
how likely they are to be false;
how badly the project fails if they are false.
A polished objective may suddenly reveal a dozen untested dependencies.
Good. That is information you needed before development.
Conduct a premortem
Use Gary Klein’s premortem technique:
It is 18 months from now. The course was built, learners passed, and the performance metric did not move. Write the postmortem.
Language models are good at this because it turns an evidentiary problem into a narrative task.
The result is not proof. It is a list of failure hypotheses you can investigate before spending the budget.
Interrogate real data
This is where the value rises sharply.
Provide actual inputs:

• ticket categories

• quality scorecards

• error logs

• observation note

• customer complaints

• interview transcripts

• audit findings

• workflow data
Then ask the system to identify patterns, cluster possible causes, compare groups, locate anomalies, and separate supported conclusions from unsupported ones.
One question should be standard:
What conclusions does this evidence not support?
That question is often more valuable than asking what the data proves.
Audit alignment at scale
Give the system 40 objectives and their corresponding assessments.
Ask which assessments fail to measure the objective.
Ask which objectives have no practice.
Ask where criteria vary without explanation.
Ask which lessons teach content that appears nowhere in the assessment or objectives.
This is verification, not validation. But it is useful verification, and humans miss these things when the volume gets high.
Pressure-test criteria
Do not ask AI to supply the number.
Ask it to challenge the number:
Here is the proposed criterion of 90%. What five questions must be answered before this threshold is defensible?
That turns the fabrication risk into an interrogation.
Enforce language discipline
AI reliably catches verbs such as:

• understand

• know

• appreciate

• become aware of

• learn
Those verbs often conceal the absence of an observable behavior.
It is a small function. It is also nearly free.
